claims.text: Dean's keynote at the 2009 workshop on large scale distributed systems carried a table titled Numbers Everyone Should Know, giving order-of-magnitude latencies: a cache reference at the first level around 0.5 nanoseconds, a branch mispredict around 5, a main memory reference around 100, sending 2 kilobytes over a gigabit network around 20,000, reading 1 megabyte sequentially from memory around 250,000, a round trip within the same datacenter around 500,000, a disk seek around 10,000,000, and reading 1 megabyte sequentially from disk around 30,000,000.

source.title: Jeffrey Dean, Large-Scale Distributed Systems at Google: Current Systems and Future Directions, keynote at LADIS 2009, October 2009 — the slide deck carrying Numbers Everyone Should Know

claims.text: A takeaway frequently drawn from that table is that writes to the network within a datacenter are much faster than writes to local disk.

source.title: Jeffrey Dean, Large-Scale Distributed Systems at Google: Current Systems and Future Directions, keynote at LADIS 2009, October 2009 — the slide deck carrying Numbers Everyone Should Know

claims.text: Bandwidth improves much more quickly than latency across disks, networks, memories and processors, with bandwidth improving by more than the square of the improvement in latency — so the two quantities in any estimate age at different rates.

source.title: David A. Patterson, Latency lags bandwidth, Communications of the ACM 47(10):71-75, October 2004

beats.broke: a design decision has a cost that will only be discovered after it is built, and the alternatives differ by factors large enough that guessing wrongly is expensive
beats.fix: estimate before building, using order-of-magnitude figures and arithmetic rather than precision — the purpose is to tell a hundred apart from a hundred thousand, not to be accurate
beats.cost: the figures age at different rates and some of them age fast, so an estimate built on memorised constants is wrong in a way that is invisible until the constants are checked
beats.interview: what a back-of-the-envelope estimate is actually for
